about: Military reforms to 1 AD (decisions 'Military reforms', 'Which army reforms first', 'What makes a reform available', 'What reforms cost', 'Refusing a reform', 'Who is angered by reforms'). Each belongs to a realm (civ). The realm that plays it is offered it when history's cause is present and it knows the technology (if one is named); other realms take it in the year history did. cost: talents; years: until it takes effect; rival: points the rival faction gains. cause kinds: at_war_years (at war that many years), at_war_with (a realm), manpower_low (under a quarter of what it could call up), defeat (a heavy defeat in the last ten years), defeat_by (by a realm), defeat_or_manpower, unrest_culture (a restless province of that people), pirates (pirates at sea), after_civil_war (a loyal army turned on the realm), holds_culture (a province of that people), fought_culture (a battle against that people in the last ten years), no_war_years (peace that long). effects: manpower and upkeep scale the realm's call-up and army pay; loyalty_rate speeds how fast armies grow loyal to their generals; veterans_paid pays veterans in silver from the treasury instead of land; might_<arm>, garrison and unrest as for technologies. Sources as given; our own summary, free for any use.

reforms.name: The velites
reforms.text: In the war with Hannibal the youngest and poorest were trained as light troops riding behind the cavalry; they became the velites.

reforms.name: Scipio's Spanish drill
reforms.text: Scipio drilled his legions at New Carthage and took up the Spanish sword.

reforms.name: Gaius Gracchus' military law
reforms.text: The state clothes its soldiers at no cost to them, and no one under seventeen may be enlisted.

reforms.name: The Marian reforms
reforms.text: Marius enlisted the landless poor as volunteers and armed them at the state's cost; the legion fought in cohorts and carried its own baggage. The soldiers looked to their general for land.

reforms.name: Citizenship for the Italian allies
reforms.text: After the Social War the allies became citizens, and their soldiers served in the legions.

reforms.name: The Gabinian command at sea
reforms.text: Pompey was given 500 ships and three years to clear the sea of pirates; he did it in three months.

reforms.name: The standing army of Augustus
reforms.text: Fixed terms of service and a military treasury that paid veterans in silver instead of land; the legions looked to the emperor, not their generals.

reforms.name: Egyptians in the phalanx
reforms.text: Ptolemy IV armed and drilled 20,000 Egyptians as phalangites; they won Raphia, then turned their arms against the dynasty.

reforms.name: The Seleucid cataphracts
reforms.text: After his march to the east Antiochus III armoured horse and rider in mail on the Parthian model.

reforms.name: Antiochus IV's Roman-armed men
reforms.text: At the parade at Daphne 5,000 men marched armed in the Roman fashion.

reforms.name: Philip V's rebuilding of Macedon
reforms.text: After Cynoscephalae Philip moved Thracians into Macedon and urged his people to raise children, so that the land would have soldiers again.

reforms.name: The thureos shield
reforms.text: After the Galatian invasion Greek armies took up the long oval Celtic shield and fought as thureophoroi.

reforms.name: Cleomenes' revolution at Sparta
reforms.text: Cleomenes cancelled debts, made 4,000 new citizens of the perioikoi, and armed them with the Macedonian pike.

reforms.name: Nabis frees the helots
reforms.text: Nabis freed slaves and helots and filled his army with them and with mercenaries.

reforms.name: Hiero's army and Archimedes' engines
reforms.text: Hiero II built a citizen army and walls, and Archimedes armed them with engines that held Rome off for two years.

reforms.name: Pyrrhus' mixed line
reforms.text: Against Rome Pyrrhus set Italian companies between the sections of his phalanx.

reforms.name: The drill of Xanthippus
reforms.text: A Spartan mercenary drilled Carthage's army and taught it to fight Rome on open ground with elephants and horse.

reforms.name: The Barcid army of Spain
reforms.text: Hamilcar, Hasdrubal and Hannibal raised a professional army in Spain, bound to their family more than to the city.

reforms.name: Masinissa's kingdom
reforms.text: Masinissa settled his people as farmers and built a kingdom with infantry and elephants as well as horse.

reforms.name: Juba's Roman-trained legions
reforms.text: Juba I drilled Numidian foot in the Roman manner, in cohorts.

reforms.name: Mithridates' Roman-style army
reforms.text: After Sulla's victories Mithridates gave up gilded show-arms and had Roman exiles drill his men as legions.

reforms.name: The army of Tigranes the Great
reforms.text: Tigranes raised a vast army of cataphracts and levies from the peoples he conquered.

reforms.name: Burebista unites the Getae
reforms.text: Burebista united the Getae and Dacians and could put 200,000 men in the field.

reforms.name: Viriathus' way of war
reforms.text: A shepherd turned general, Viriathus beat Roman armies for eight years by feigned flight and ambush.

reforms.name: Vercingetorix's levy
reforms.text: Vercingetorix fixed each people's quota of men and arms, enforced it harshly, and burned the land before the Romans.
